thread.title: Market Snapshot: U.S. stock futures search for a catalyst as earnings stay in focus

title: Market Snapshot: U.S. stock futures search for a catalyst as earnings stay in focus
text:
1:40 p.m. ET Share 
Philip Morris on track for worst trading day since being spun off Getty Images Ryan Vlastelica Markets reporter 
U.S. stocks fell on Thursday, with major indexes dropping in a broad decline as investors digested a fresh round of corporate earnings. 
While results have largely come in ahead of expectations thus far this reporting season, there have been some disappointments, and others haven’t produced the kind of blowout results seen necessary to continue pushing shares higher from elevated levels. 
Stocks extended their decline as Treasurys sold off, pushing the yield on the 10-year note TMUBMUSD10Y, +1.42% to a 2018 high. Rising yields, however, were seen providing a lift for bank stocks. What are the main benchmarks doing? 
The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, -0.49% was down 170 points, or 0.7%, 24,580, with the day’s decline pushing the blue-chip average back into negative territory for the year . The S&P 500 SPX, -0.73% lost 25 points, or 0.9%, to 2,684, dropping back below its 50-day moving average. The Nasdaq Composite Index COMP, -0.82% lost 74 points to 7,221, a decline of 1%. 
Ten of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors were lower on the day. The biggest loser was consumer staples, which slumped 3.5% following weak results from tobacco giant Philip Morris, as well as an acquisition by Procter & Gamble. The staples sector was on track for its biggest one-day drop since Feb. 5 . 
Financials were the sole industry group trading to the upside. It rose 1.1% on the day. What’s driving markets? 
First-quarter earnings reports have grabbed investors’ attention this week, with Netflix Inc. NFLX, -0.68% Goldman Sachs Group Inc. GS, +0.02% and UnitedHealth Group Inc. UNH, -0.29% among the companies that have posted encouraging results. 
See: Goldman was king of the quarter, but Morgan is the one to buy, analysts say 
The S&P 500 components are expected to see earnings growth of 17.3% for the period , the fastest rate of expansion since 2011. The results have been enough to largely overshadow such uncertainties as trade policy questions and tensions over Syria. What are strategists saying? 
“There’s a growing fear that the good news we’ve seen over the past years is coming to an end, that we’re closer to a meaningful downturn in the economy than we had previously been expecting,” said Peter Kenny, senior market strategist at Global Markets Advisory Group. 
“Earnings have been extremely strong, and data have been extremely strong, but that’s not resulting in any enthusiasm for stocks. Confidence has been shaken by the price action over the past two months, and there’s a lot of uncertainty.” Which stocks are in focus? 
Shares in tobacco giant   tumbled 16% after the company posted weaker-than-expected revenue , along with a stronger-than-anticipated adjusted profit. The stock was on track for its biggest one-day percentage decline since being spun off from Altria Group Inc. MO, -6.91% in 2008. Altria fell 6.9%. 
Shares in Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, +1.67% rose 1.7% after CEO Jeff Bezos disclosed in an annual letter to shareholders that the e-commerce juggernaut’s Amazon Prime subscription program has topped 100 million members world-wide . 
And see: Bezos wants Amazon workers to start meetings reading memos ‘with the clarity of angels singing’ 
Technology stocks were broadly lower, with chip makers particularly weak. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. TSM, -5.94% gave an outlook that was below expectations , raising questions about demand for the overall industry. Separately, reports late Wednesday that Facebook Inc. FB, +0.78% plans to design chips , providing another headwind for the sector. 
The VanEck Vectors Semiconductor ETF SMH, -4.18% lost 3.9%. Among major chip makers, Advanced Micro Devices AMD, -2.54% fell 2.9% and Nvidia Corp. NVDA, -3.29% was off 3.5%. 
Also weighing on tech was Apple Inc. AAPL, -2.17% which shed 2.5%. 
Procter & Gamble Co. ’s stock PG, -3.21% sank 3.6% after the consumer-products giant agreed to acquire a consumer-health business from Germany’s Merck KGaA MRK, +0.32% in a $4.2 billion deal . P&G also posted quarterly results that beat forecasts . 
Shares in credit-card company American Express Co. AXP, +6.42% climbed 5.8% a day after reporting stronger-than-expected results. The stock was on track for its best one-day performance since October 2016. 
Bank of New York Mellon Corp . BK, +4.84% reported first-quarter earnings and revenue that topped expectations . Shares rose 4.2%, helping to support the financial sector. 
Both stocks were among the biggest gainers in the financial sector, which appeared to benefit from the rise in yields. Rising long-dated yields are seen as a tailwind for bank profitability. 
Blackstone Group LP BX, +1.74% reported first-quarter earnings that topped expectations . Shares rose 1.2%. 
Aceto Corp. ACET, -63.38% dropped 64% after the developer of health products and pharmaceutical ingredients maker said it was negotiating credit agreement waivers with its lenders , cutting its dividend, taking a large impairment charge and initiating an evaluation of strategic alternatives. 
Roku Inc. ROKU, +4.05% rose 3.8% after an analyst from Needham played down the potential impact of a deal that would see Amazon.com Inc. sell some products at Best Buy Co Inc . BBY, -2.65% Which economic reports are in focus? 
Initial jobless claims declined 1,000 to 232,000 in the latest week . While analyst had expected a somewhat steeper decline, claims remain near a 45-year low. 
The Philadelphia Federal Reserve’s business-conditions index came in at 23.2 in April. 
Check out: MarketWatch’s Economic Calendar 
Federal Reserve Board Gov. Lael Brainard said there are “some signs of financial imbalances in the economy,” citing asset valuations and business leverage . 
At 6:45 p.m. Eastern, Cleveland Fed President Loretta Mester should give a speech on the economic outlook and policy at the University of Pittsburgh’s business school. What are other markets doing?
